<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The older adult population is increasing rapidly and experiences a multitude of chronic conditions affecting quality of life. Physical activity and reduced sedentary behavior reduce adverse health conditions and help preserve functional independence and cognitive abilities, but the older adult age group has much lower levels of physical activity than recommended compared with other population demographics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study aimed to understand older adults’ motivations toward health and physical activity and the role of technology in achieving their health and physical activity goals and to explore the attitudes toward the use of generative AI in health apps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was qualitative and based on hour-long interviews with 20 older adults living in the United States. To elicit specific design preferences, participants were presented with visual probes of AI-generated avatars. The interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, and the coding process drew on reflexive and grounded theory techniques.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults primarily wished to maintain functional independence, both physical and cognitive, prioritizing baseline maintenance rather than continuous optimization. They reported satisfaction with levels of physical activity, adjusting them to chronic conditions and injuries. They were active through everyday functions of living as well as structured exercise programs with many participants using wearable devices and smartphones to help monitor their activity. They reported being motivated by social accountability and gamification, although some found the latter condescending or anxiety-inducing. Accessibility issues were mentioned frequently, including problems with touchscreens, limited viewing, difficulty navigating interfaces with clutter, complex multitouch processes for undertaking actions, and steep learning curves. Computers were preferred for certain tasks over mobile phones due to easier viewability, keyboard access, and greater security features. Personalization was highly desired in health apps. There was a willingness to use more health technology, including generative AI, and they were willing to consider AI in both motivational and informational roles in apps as long as it was personalized. AI embodiment preferences varied widely but with an emphasis on relatability. However, there was marked skepticism toward data privacy, concerns about the loss of independence and self-efficacy, and doubts about AI’s accuracy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults are primarily motivated by sustaining functional independence, although accessibility barriers in current health apps remain. Participants were open to AI for physical activity support, but expectations varied. They viewed AI as a passive “tool,” a directive “coach,” or a relational “companion.” Considerable variation in preferences for gamification and visual design suggested that future apps require greater modularity. As skepticism over data privacy and AI accuracy remains high, greater transparency and explainability might be needed to engender trust.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Motivations, Barriers, and the Potential of AI in Physical Activity Apps for US Older Adults: Interview Study

                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Health care systems increasingly offer services to citizens through online portals, which have been found to be associated with patient satisfaction and better management of health concerns. Few studies have compared self-reported use with objectively documented portal use, especially among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine differences between documented and self-reported health portal use, and their associations with background variables and digital health literacy (DHL) among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted among 600 participants aged 60 years and older, who were sampled from a registry of members of a national health maintenance organization (HMO). The participants reported their use of the HMO’s portal, their DHL, and demographic and background variables. Participants’ use of the portal was retrospectively retrieved from the HMO’s administrative database.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A large gap between self-reported use and documented use of the health portal was found: for example, while only 8.1% (46/566) reported not using the portal, the HMO’s records indicated that 62% (372/600) did not make use of the portal. However, a positive correlation was found between self-reported use and documented use (

                      =0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Significant positive associations were found between administrative and physician-related online services, both reported use (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.41;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and documented use (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.56;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). A multivariate analysis, where documented use was the dependent variable, explained 12.5% of the variance. Experience with computers (β=0.13;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02) and ethnicity (β=−0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) were significantly associated with documented use. DHL, though significantly associated with documented use at the bivariate level (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.09;
                      <jats:italic>P=</jats:italic>
                      .04), was not significantly associated with documented use in this analysis (β=0.02;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.97).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that users tend to overestimate their health portal use. Interpretations vary from measurement issues, such as social desirability bias regarding digital functioning or the perception that assisted use also constitutes usage, to signaling their identity as engaged digital health consumers. Future studies on digital health use should also include measures of electronically documented use and not only self-reported use.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychological richness, a dimension of well-being characterized by novelty, complexity, and perspective change, is theoretically grounded in varied and unusual experiences. This study examined whether daily activity diversity was associated with psychological richness in two cohorts of midlife and older adults from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daily reports were drawn from two cohorts of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: MIDUS 2 (M2; N = 1,834) and the MIDUS Refresher (MR; N = 730). Daily activity diversity was quantified with Shannon entropy, capturing both the breadth and evenness of participants' daily activities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower activity diversity was associated with higher psychological richness in both cohorts (M2: β = −0.07, p &lt;.001; MR: β = −0.06, p = .009). After adjustment for age, sex, education, race, and chronic health conditions, associations were inverse in both cohorts but statistically significant only in M2 (M2: β = −0.07, p &lt;.001; MR: β = −0.04, p = .068).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that broader activity repertoires do not necessarily correspond to greater psychological richness and that psychologically rich lives may coexist with relatively narrow patterns of daily engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Activity diversity and psychological richness across midlife and older adulthood

records.abstract: <jats:p>Hypertension is highly prevalent among adults aged 45 years and older in India, yet limited evidence exists on the combined associations of waist circumference (WC) and body mass index (BMI) with hypertension. This study examined their independent and joint associations with hypertension using Wave 1 (2017–18) of the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) among 59,658 adults aged 45 years and older. Hypertension was defined as measured blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations across combined WC–BMI categories. Overall hypertension prevalence was 31.3%. Individuals with normal BMI but large WC had higher odds of hypertension (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.37; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.19–1.58). Obese individuals with large WC had the highest odds (AOR = 1.77; 95% CI: 1.45–2.17). Both central and general obesity were independently associated with hypertension. Routine WC assessment alongside BMI may improve identification of high-risk individuals in India’s middle-aged and older population.</jats:p>
title: Beyond BMI: The Role of Abdominal Obesity in Hypertension Risk Among Adults Aged 45 Years and Older in India

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model

                    <jats:p>While WHO ICOPE screening is routine, the association between multi-domain intrinsic capacity (IC) decline and falls remains understudied in community-based gerontology practice.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study analysed 775 rural older adults (mean age 79.4) with ≥1 IC abnormality using multivariable logistic regression and dose–response analysis to evaluate fall risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Nutrition (aOR = 5.10), mobility (aOR = 2.60), depression (aOR = 2.34), and vision (aOR = 2.21) impairments were independently associated with falls. Fall rates rose monotonically from 4.6% (one domain) to 29.1% (≥4 domains; p
                      <jats:sub>trend</jats:sub>

                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An IC impairment count of ≥3, or specific clusters (nutrition, mobility, depression), provides practical triage criteria for community-based fall-prevention. These findings facilitate person-centred risk stratification and resource allocation within integrated care systems for super-aging societies.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.</jats:p>
title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study

records.abstract: <jats:p>Dementia prevention is receiving increasing attention considering the surge in number of dementia incidence worldwide. Although there are modifiable risk factors, the public remains largely unaware of dementia prevention. Many individuals turn to online platforms such as YouTube for health-related information, where content can shape beliefs, attitudes, and decision-making. However, little is known about how people interpret and discuss dementia prevention in these digital spaces. This study aimed to explore how dementia prevention is perceived by the public, as reflected in user generated comments posted on YouTube videos related to dementia prevention. A qualitative thematic analysis was conducted by examining comments from YouTube videos identified through Google Advanced Search. Twenty-six videos were selected based on predefined criteria, and comments were extracted and cleaned prior to analysis. Engagement metrics, including views, likes, and replies, were also examined to understand how users interacted with the content. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic approach. A total of 7314 comments were retrieved from 26 videos. Following data cleaning and removal of ineligible comments, 2034 comments were included for final analysis. Thematic analysis revealed three themes: (i) fear and perceived vulnerability to dementia; (ii) perceptions of dementia risk factors; and (iii) trust and credibility of dementia prevention information. These themes revealed fear, modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors, and both public reliance on and distrust of scientific evidence. YouTube provides an important platform for public discussion about dementia prevention. Although it offers opportunities to increase awareness, viewer comments reflected inconsistent understandings and conflicting beliefs about dementia prevention, highlighting the need for clear, evidence-based communication to improve public understanding.</jats:p>
title: Perceptions of Dementia Prevention on YouTube: A Thematic Analysis of Viewer Comments

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Major lower extremity amputation for diabetic foot complications is associated with substantial mortality, particularly in older adults. We evaluated whether routinely available preoperative laboratory parameters provide prognostic information for 24-month mortality and developed an exploratory laboratory-based risk score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective cohort study included 72 patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent transtibial or transfemoral amputation for diabetic foot complications between January 2021 and June 2023 at a tertiary referral center. Vital status was ascertained through July 31, 2025. Associations with 24-month all-cause mortality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. A 3-point score was derived from laboratory predictors using receiver operating characteristic analysis and Youden-index-based thresholds. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed, and bootstrap optimism correction was applied to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. The proposed score was additionally compared with the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), and Hemoglobin–Albumin–Lymphocyte–Platelet (HALP) score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Thirty-nine patients (54.2%) died within 24 months. Kaplan–Meier-estimated 24-month survival was 45.8% (95% CI 34.1–56.8%). In multivariable Cox analysis, higher hemoglobin (adjusted HR 1.302, 95% CI 1.041–1.628;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.021), lower platelet count (adjusted HR 0.9966, 95% CI 0.9939–0.9994;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.017), and lower albumin (adjusted HR 0.868, 95% CI 0.813–0.927;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) were independently associated with mortality. One point was assigned for hemoglobin > 10.3 g/dL, platelet count < 342.5 × 10⁹/L, and albumin < 28.5 g/L. Patients with scores ≥ 2 had substantially lower 24-month survival than those with scores 0–1 (8.0% vs. 66.0%; log-rank
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). The score had an AUC of 0.798 for 24-month mortality. The underlying Cox model had an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.712. The score showed numerically higher discrimination than GNRI (AUC 0.739) and PNI (0.735), and higher discrimination than HALP (0.590).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A simple score based on albumin, hemoglobin, and platelet count showed promising prognostic discrimination for 24-month mortality after major amputation in this geriatric diabetic foot cohort. Quantitative ischemia severity and standardized neuropathy and frailty assessments were unavailable, and the score was derived and evaluated in the same derivation cohort, while bootstrap optimism correction was limited to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. It should therefore be regarded as exploratory, should not replace comprehensive clinical and vascular assessment, and requires external validation before clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development of an exploratory preoperative laboratory-based score for 24-month mortality after major lower extremity amputation in geriatric diabetic foot patients

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malnutrition is highly prevalent in geriatric trauma patients and is associated with impaired recovery, complications, and reduced likelihood of returning home. Nonetheless, the impact of a targeted protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay on patient outcome and rehabilitation remains to be investigated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This single-center randomized controlled study enrolled patients ≥ 70 years with fragility fractures admitted to a Level I trauma center. Nutritional status was assessed using the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Patients screened positive in ≥ 1 tool were classified as being at nutritional risk and randomized to a protein-enriched diet (Group A) or standard diet (Group B); patients with negative screening served as observational reference group without nutritional risk (Group C). The intervention targeted 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein. Primary outcomes were in-hospital medical complications, surgical site infections and functional mobility at discharge. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, discharge destination, and in-hospital mortality. Multinomial logistic regression assessed independent associations with discharge destination.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Of the 218 patients (mean age 81.8 ± 6.9 years; 72.0% female), 100 (45.9%) screened positive for being at nutritional risk and were randomized to intervention (A,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 46) or control (B,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 54), while 118 (54.1%) patients without nutritional risk served as reference group (C). Patients at nutritional risk showed higher comorbidity burdens, higher ASA classes, and greater frailty than group C. Medical complications occurred in 45.0% of patients, with no significant differences between groups. Serum albumin decreased and CRP increased during hospitalization, without differences among the groups. Patients in reference group C were more often independently mobile and discharged home, whereas all patients at nutritional risk more frequently required institutional care. In multivariable analysis, a higher age-adjusted CCI was independently associated with discharge destination, whereas no independent effect of the nutritional intervention was observed.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this geriatric trauma cohort, being at nutritional risk was closely linked to frailty and multimorbidity. A protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay did not translate into measurable short-term benefits regarding complications, functional mobility, length of stay or discharge destination. Nutritional risk should therefore be considered within the broader context of overall vulnerability, and nutritional care may need to be embedded in comprehensive longitudinal rehabilitation strategies extending beyond the acute in-hospital phase.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on 12 May 2026 (NCT07582575).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity is common in older adults and has been associated with adverse cognitive outcomes. However, findings remain heterogeneous because of differences in multimorbidity definitions, cognitive measures, and study designs. This review aimed to synthesize evidence on the association between multimorbidity and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature sources were searched up to August 2026. Observational studies examining multimorbidity, defined as ≥ 2 chronic conditions, and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years were included. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized narratively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall, greater multimorbidity burden was generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, while several specific multimorbidity patterns, particularly cardiometabolic and cardiovascular patterns, were associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, or dementia. However, some studies reported null or domain-specific associations. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across multimorbidity definitions, cognitive assessments, study designs, populations, and confounding adjustment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity may be associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in older adults, but the strength and consistency of the evidence vary across studies. Interpretation is limited by methodological heterogeneity, potential risk of bias, and the observational nature of the evidence. More standardized prospective studies are needed to clarify these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although greater life enjoyment is associated with a lower risk of frailty, little is known about the association between sources of life enjoyment and frailty. This study investigated the associations between the variety and types of sources of enjoyment in life (“enjoyment sources”) and frailty among community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted using data from a community-based cohort study in Japan. In 2020, questionnaires were mailed to 4,996 randomly selected adults aged ≥65 years, and 2,764 responded. Follow-up questionnaires were sent to 1,635 consenting participants in 2023, with 904 responses obtained. Frailty was assessed using a 5-item self-report questionnaire at baseline and follow-up. Enjoyment sources were assessed through yes/no and open-ended questions at baseline and categorized using content analysis. The number of identified categories was counted, and participants were classified into no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional analysis included 2,361 participants, and the prevalence of frailty was 26.6%, 16.7%, and 11.3% in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. Cross-sectional analyses showed that a greater variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of both prefrailty and frailty. In the 3-year longitudinal analysis, 688 participants were included. Among them, incident frailty occurred in 20.2%, 11.1%, and 10.0% of participants in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. The variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of incident frailty in both crude and basic adjusted models. The odds ratios for the single-source and multiple-source groups were similar. Exploratory analysis of the 10 most frequently reported enjoyment sources showed that books, sports, friends, foods, and singing/playing musical instruments showed inverse trends with frailty, whereas media consumption showed a positive trend with frailty in unadjusted cross-sectional trend tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Having one or more enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of frailty among community-dwelling older adults in both cross-sectional and 3-year longitudinal analyses. The exploratory analysis also suggested that the associations between specific types of enjoyment sources and frailty may differ.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The decline in musculoskeletal function with aging is a key contributor to mobility impairments and loss of independence. While sarcopenia and dynapenia are well described, recent evidence highlights muscle power as a more sensitive indicator of functional deterioration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to compare age-associated differences in muscle mass, force, and lower-limb muscle power in older adults over different assessment methods, while accounting for sex-related differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three hundred nineteen community-dwelling adults aged 60–97 years were assessed for muscle mass (DXA-derived lean mass, appendicular skeletal muscle mass index), muscle force (handgrip force, knee extension maximal isometric contraction), muscle moments and angular velocity (isokinetic dynamometry), and lower-limb muscle power (isokinetic testing and sit-to-stand power). Associations with age and sex were examined using regression models and ANOVA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Lower-limb muscle power showed a stronger negative association with age than muscle force or mass (β = − 0.433 vs. − 0.303 and − 0.119, respectively;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). However, the present study could not determine whether muscle power begins to decline earlier than muscle force or mass. For several variables, age associations were stronger in males than in females, most consistently for lower-limb power, although these interactions were not systematically reproduced in age-stratified analyses. The strongest negative age associations were observed between 71 and 80 years, whereas fewer significant associations (only for handgrip) were observed after age 80.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower-limb muscle power appeared more sensitive to age-associated differences than muscle force or mass, supporting its role as a key biomarker of neuromuscular aging. This study also highlights that sex may contribute to variability in age-associated patterns of muscle power, raising questions about the universality of its definition that warrant further confirmation. These findings emphasize the clinical importance of including power assessments in strategies to preserve independence in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05343286,
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286" ext-link-type="uri">https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286</jats:ext-link>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Age-associated differences in lower-extremity muscle mass, force, and power in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis of sex differences

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design and setting</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Measurements</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (< 295 mOsmol/l). Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy) and agreement (Cohen’s κ) were calculated. Glucose was compared between concordant/discordant groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001 for planned pairwise comparisons).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dysphagia is a critical geriatric syndrome associated with an increased risk of aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and mortality in older adults. The aim of this study was to evaluate the associations between Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) parameters and dysphagia risk (Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10) ≥ 3) in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 468 community-dwelling older adults presenting to a geriatric outpatient clinic. Participants with severe cognitive impairment, Parkinson’s disease, those residing in a nursing home, and those with an acute medical condition were excluded from the study. Dysphagia risk was assessed using the EAT-10; probable sarcopenia was defined according to the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2019 (EWGSOP2) criteria; depressive symptoms were evaluated with the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15); and nutritional status was assessed using the Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF). Independent risk factors were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the final multivariate regression model, the presence of probable sarcopenia (OR = 2.654, 95% CI: 1.184–5.947,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.018) and higher GDS-15 scores (OR = 1.155, 95% CI: 1.063–1.255,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001) were independently and significantly associated with dysphagia risk. In contrast, a one-point increase in the MNA-SF score (indicating better nutritional status), when treated as a continuous variable, was an independent protective factor against dysphagia risk (OR = 0.684, 95% CI: 0.521–0.897,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.006).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In community-dwelling older adults, probable sarcopenia and depressive symptoms significantly increase the dysphagia risk, whereas good nutritional status plays a protective role. Prior to the development of dysphagia and its associated complications, optimizing muscle strength, mood, and nutritional status in outpatient settings is of importance for maintaining swallowing safety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The sample included
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The COVID-19 pandemic disproportionately affected older adults (aged 65 years and older) due to age-related physiological vulnerabilities and forced social isolation. This study systematically evaluates the public health response and management strategies executed for older populations across two highly contrasting macroeconomic and governance structures: Cameroon, a Lower-Middle Income Country (LMIC), and the United States, a High-Income Country (HIC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review and structured SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis were conducted in strict accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We systematically queried PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and African Journals Online (AJOL) for peer-reviewed literature, legal acts, and official institutional frameworks published between January 2020 and February 2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-two unique sources met all predefined inclusion criteria. Cameroon’s operational response drew heavily from highly decentralized, resilient community/kinship networks and immediate, government-mandated financial cushions, such as a 20% expansion in state pensions. However, these baseline mitigation efforts were severely restricted by deep structural healthcare weaknesses, a 73% fear-driven clinical avoidance rate, extreme diagnostic deficits (10.02 tests per 1,000 population), and resource constraints inside active conflict zones. Conversely, the United States leveraged massive technological capital, real-time molecular surveillance networks, and rapid mRNA vaccine rollouts that effectively averted an estimated 92% of potential deaths among older adults’ post-implementation, alongside a massive expansion of telehealth serving 59% of isolated seniors. Nevertheless, the United States response suffered from profound, catastrophic infection control failures within long-term care facilities, intense socio-political policy polarization and deep-seated institutionalized racial health inequities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future global pandemic preparedness frameworks must systematically integrate targeted “healthy aging” strategies directly into statutory national health policy architectures. This study demonstrates that isolated country analyses mask systemic vulnerabilities: HICs fail due to decentralization and polarization despite high GDP, while LMICs can innovate social resilience but remain strictly bottle-necked by material supply chains. Global preparedness metrics must abandon static spending indices in favor of structural equity and operational flexibility frameworks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical trial number: not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Past-year hospitalization reports may identify older adults with adverse subsequent prognosis, but two assessments do not continuously observe hospital use and their incremental information beyond one-wave reporting is uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analysed two three-wave windows of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS): 2011 (Wave 1) and 2013 (Wave 2) hospitalization reports with 2015 (Wave 3) outcomes, and 2013 (Wave 2) and 2015 (Wave 3) reports with 2018 (Wave 4) outcomes. Patterns were 00 (neither assessment), 01 (second only), 10 (first only) and 11 (both). The prespecified primary analysis compared 11 with 00 for survivor-conditional ADL deterioration (increase ≥1) among participants with observed outcome-assessment ADL. Modified Poisson models used community-clustered robust covariance and 50 multiply imputed datasets. Four-pattern, one-wave, mortality, composite, sequential complete-covariate, cognition missing-not-at-random (MNAR), and inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW) analyses were also examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ADL deterioration occurred in 932/4,365 observed survivors in Window 1 and 961/4,911 in Window 2. Adjusted RRs for 11 versus 00 were 1.230 (95% CI 1.007–1.502) and 1.094 (0.906–1.320), respectively. RRs for 11 versus pooled 01 + 10 were 1.229 (1.000–1.511) and 1.019 (0.845–1.228). Mortality RRs were 1.461 (0.986–2.166) and 1.482 (1.187–1.849), and death-or-deterioration RRs were 1.240 (1.054–1.459) and 1.166 (1.031–1.319). In fixed complete-covariate sequential analyses, 11-versus-00 point estimates moved markedly toward or below the null after multidimensional health adjustment, with wide confidence intervals. Cognition MNAR estimates changed little; IPCW point estimates were similar in magnitude (Window 1 RR 1.222, 95% CI 0.999–1.494; Window 2 RR 1.092, 0.905–1.317).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 11 pattern marked less favorable prognosis relative to 00, but the survivor-conditional functional association varied across calendar windows and analytic strategies, and two reports did not consistently distinguish risk from one-wave reporting. These related within-cohort windows do not constitute independent replication. Results support cautious prognostic interpretation, not a causal effect, verified recurrent-admission measure or stand-alone screening rule.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Two-assessment patterns of past-year hospitalization reporting and subsequent functional deterioration and mortality among older adults in China: a two-window longitudinal prognostic factor study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Family participation and teamwork are crucial components of person-centred dementia care in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) and are therefore widely recommended. Each period will last 7 months, separated by a 1-month washout. Clusters will follow one of two sequences (intervention → usual care or usual care → intervention).                     <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical disorders frequently co-occur with psychological and cognitive conditions, increasing the risk of disability.                     <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were obtained from the 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, involving 5186 adults aged 60 and older with a 2-year follow-up.                     <jats:p>Five disease patterns were identified: only physical disorders, psychological or cognitive disorders, physical-cognitive multimorbidity, physical-psychological multimorbidity, and physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity. Specifically, physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity presented the highest risk (aRR = 4.02, 95%CI:2.94–5.50), followed by physical-psychological multimorbidity (aRR = 3.30, 95%CI:2.40–4.54), physical-cognitive multimorbidity (aRR = 2.20, 95%CI:1.60–3.03), and only physical disorders (aRR = 1.85, 95%CI:1.36–2.52).                     <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) carries a poor prognosis, and older patients and those with impaired performance status are often underrepresented in randomized trials. This study evaluated real-world treatment patterns, survival outcomes, and factors associated with outcome in older patients with GBM.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively analyzed 63 patients aged ≥ 65 years with a diagnosis of GBM managed at a single-center radiation oncology department between 2014 and 2023. Multivariable Cox models included age, sex, Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), radiologically confirmed gross total resection (GTR), and temozolomide (TMZ) administration as clinically prespecified covariates. Complete-case analyses were performed. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals, with additional time-varying and exploratory sensitivity analyses addressing diagnostic classification, treatment selection, concomitant TMZ exposure, and treatment timing.</jats:p>

                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 56; 50 deaths), increasing age was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.02–1.17;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sagittal imbalance in older adults causes impairments in standing and gait, leading to mobility limitations (defined as “locomotive syndrome” in Japan), which are risk factors for future long-term care needs. This study aimed to investigate whether sagittal imbalance is a risk factor for long-term care needs in older adults.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective cohort study included 552 participants from the 2010 Locomotive Syndrome and Health Outcomes in Aizu Cohort Study (LOHAS). The primary outcome was incident long-term care need, defined as a new certification in the national insurance system during a 5-year follow-up. Sagittal vertical axis (SVA) was measured on a standing whole-spine lateral radiograph. Bodily pain (SF-12) and physical function (3-m timed up and go [TUG] test) were assessed. Association between SVA and incident long-term care needs was evaluated using the Cox proportional hazards model, and hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals [CIs] were calculated, with adjustment for age, sex, pain, TUG, heart disease, and depression.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>

By SVA categories, incident care needs were observed in 9.1%, 12.7%, and 31.0% of participants in the SVA < 40, 40–95, and > 95 mm groups, respectively. The adjusted HRs [95% CI] for the SVA > 95 mm group were 2.72 [1.26–5.88] versus the SVA < 40 mm group; and 2.13 [0.97–4.70] versus the SVA 40–95 group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Severe sagittal imbalance was associated with an increased risk of incident long-term care needs in older adults.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older patients aged 70 years and above exhibit immunosenescence, increased comorbidity burden, and high susceptibility to adverse drug reactions. The standard HRZE regimen remains controversial in this population due to the considerable toxicity of pyrazinamide (PZA). This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-containing triple or quadruple regimens compared with conventional standard HR(L2)ZE or HR(L2)E regimens in older pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients, so as to provide evidence for individualized treatment strategies in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 184 newly diagnosed PTB patients aged ≥ 70 years were enrolled in this single-center retrospective study in 2023. Patients were divided into four groups according to initial anti-tuberculosis regimens: standard HR(L2)ZE quadruple therapy group, HR(L2)E triple therapy group, FQ-containing quadruple group, and FQ-containing triple group. Treatment outcomes and adverse event rates were compared among groups. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors for treatment failure and adverse events. Propensity score matching (PSM) was further performed between the standard HR(L2)ZE and FQ-containing quadruple groups to minimize baseline selection bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Significant differences in treatment success rates and overall adverse event rates were observed among the four groups (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Compared with the standard HR(L2)ZE regimen, both FQ-containing triple and quadruple regimens achieved significantly higher treatment success rates and lower risks of treatment failure and adverse events. After adjusting for age, gender, sputum smear status, and serum albumin level, FQ- containing triple and quadruple regimens remained independently associated with improved clinical safety and efficacy. In the PSM analysis, which specifically compared the HR(L2)ZE and FQ-containing quadruple groups, HR(L2)ZE therapy was associated with a significantly higher risk of adverse events (OR = 16.87, 95% CI: 4.85–70.33,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For PTB patients aged 70 years and older, the conventional HR(L2)ZE standard regimen is associated with high toxicity and limited clinical applicability. FQ-containing triple and quadruple regimens were associated with more favorable treatment outcomes, while PZA omission was associated with a lower risk of adverse events. Individualized therapeutic strategies with prudent PZA use and rational selection of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens may be considered for older patients. Given the retrospective observational design and potential selection bias, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To systematically evaluate the effects of multicomponent exercise (ME) combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from inception to June 30, 2026. Participants were older adults aged ≥ 60 years. Interventions were required to include both ME and nutritional intervention. Primary outcomes were global cognitive function and depressive symptoms. Hedges‘ g was used as the effect size measure, and a random-effects model was prespecified as the primary model for all pooled analyses. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were also performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 9 RCTs involving 1,814 participants were included. Of these, 7 studies contributed data on global cognitive function and 5 studies contributed data on depressive symptoms. Meta-analysis showed that ME combined with nutritional intervention may improve global cognitive function (
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                       = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.08 ~ 0.54) and depressive symptoms (
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      = -0.51, 95% CI: -0.93~-0.09) in older adults, but moderate-to-high heterogeneity was observed in both global cognitive function (
                      <jats:italic>I²</jats:italic>
                      = 68.54%) and depressive symptoms (
                      <jats:italic>I²</jats:italic>
                      = 63.54%) analyses. Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant between-subgroup differences by nutrition type, baseline cognitive status, or exercise modality (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       > 0.05), and only intervention duration showed a significant subgroup difference for global cognitive function (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001).

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background:Osteoporosis and fragility fractures are major causes of disability, loss of independence, institutionalization, and mortality in the oldest old. Despite their exceptionally high fracture risk, adults aged ≥80 years remain underrepresented in randomized controlled trials. Diagnosis and treatment are complicated by the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, sarcopenia, frailty, multimorbidity, cognitive and functional impairment, and competing mortality. Summary: This narrative review discusses the diagnosis, fracture-risk assessment, non-pharmacological management, and pharmacological treatment of osteoporosis in the oldest old. Bone mineral density (BMD) remains central to osteoporosis diagnosis but incompletely characterizes fracture risk at advanced age. Previous and particularly recent fractures, prevalent vertebral fractures, falls, physical performance, nutritional status, and frailty provide complementary information. Interpretation of the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool FRAX® requires particular consideration in the oldest old because competing mortality may cause 10-year fracture probabilities to plateau or decline despite increasing age-specific fracture incidence; FRAXplus® incorporates additional risk modifiers, including falls and the number and recency of previous fractures. Non-pharmacological interventions addressing nutrition, muscle function, balance, and falls complement bone-directed pharmacotherapy. Available evidence does not indicate that chronological age itself attenuates the efficacy of osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, although direct randomized fracture-endpoint evidence in adults aged ≥80 years remains limited. Risedronate and, historically, strontium ranelate provide some of the clearest fracture data specifically in this age group, whereas evidence for most other therapies derives from older-subgroup analyses, skeletal efficacy studies, observational data, or extrapolation from pivotal trials. At advanced age, renal function, cognition, mobility, adherence, caregiver support, and continuity of care increasingly influence the translation of efficacy into clinical effectiveness. Key Messages: Fracture risk in the oldest old reflects the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, frailty, sarcopenia, and functional reserve. Available evidence supports preservation of pharmacological antifracture efficacy with advancing age, but direct evidence in octogenarians and particularly nonagenarians remains scarce. Treatment feasibility and continuity of care become increasingly relevant at advanced age. Greater representation of the oldest old in clinical trials is needed, with particular attention to fracture outcomes, treatment sequencing, time to benefit, and outcomes relevant to independence and quality of life.</jats:p>
title: Osteoporosis in the Oldest Old - From Diagnosis to Treatment: A Narrative Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction Diabetic retinopathy, which occurs during extended periods of chronic hyperglycemia, is one of the main causes of vision loss. The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) plays a central role in inflammatory and angiogenic signaling, both of which contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, but its therapeutic targeting in ocular disease has been insufficiently explored. Methods We evaluated topical RAGE229, a small-molecule RAGE inhibitor, and an intravitreally administered anti-RAGE antibody in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model. At day 84, treatment effects were assessed using masked fundoscopic scoring, RT-qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and histological morphometry. Treated eyes were evaluated against both route-matched diabetic vehicle-control groups and paired contralateral vehicle-treated eyes. Results Both interventions reduced fundoscopic pathology and retinal Vegfa and Nfkb1 expression, whereas Ager showed only a non-significant downward trend. NF-κB p65 immunoreactivity was reduced by both treatments, while a significant reduction in VEGF-A immunoreactivity was detected only in the paired anti-RAGE antibody analysis. Morphometric analysis indicated attenuation of diabetes-associated retinal thinning with both interventions. Neither intervention altered systemic glycemic control. Although both interventions demonstrated similar overall anatomical protection, anti-RAGE antibody treatment showed more consistent effects across protein-level and structural endpoints. Conclusion These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that local RAGE-targeted treatment may attenuate vascular, molecular, and structural manifestations of early experimental diabetic retinopathy without detectable changes in systemic glycemia. Further preclinical studies should evaluate ocular exposure, direct target engagement, functional visual outcomes, and reproducibility in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
title: Local RAGE Inhibition Attenuates Early Diabetic Retinal Pathology in Streptozotocin-Induced Rats

records.abstract: <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. Methods: Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). Results: Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. Conclusions: Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.</jats:p>
title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as objective indicators of mobility.</jats:p>

                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of objective impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p &lt; 0.05). Stratified analyses showed that physical activity was positively associated with IC among females, urban residents, foreign-born participants, and US-born participants, while having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC across most subgroups. Among the interactions examined, only the association between physical activity and IC differed significantly by gender (p &lt; 0.05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses
